headline: 75 Feet on Sea Girt Reef: Sea Bass Steady, Klondike Tuna Stay Ghosts
subhead: The reef bite is doing the heavy lifting this week while the deep water off Barnegat Ridge and the Klondike keeps its tuna scattered and hard to pin down.
body_markdown:
71.2 degrees. That's what the offshore buoy off our coast was reading this week, with a lazy 3.9-foot swell running at a 5-second period. That's not a number that scares anybody off the water — it's a number that tells you the reef structure is still fishing warm-water patterns, but the top of the water column is starting to lose its edge. That's the story of mid-September on this stretch of the Jersey coast: the sea bass bite on the reef network is steady and dependable, the deep-water tuna game is a lottery ticket, and the calendar is quietly setting up the next phase of the season.

Start with what's working. Sea Girt Reef, sitting in that 70-to-80-foot band depending where you drop, has been the most consistent stop in the book this week. Sea bass to 3 pounds are coming over the rail on double-hook rigs tipped with Gulp Grubs in nuclear chicken and white, fished tight to the high relief pieces on the up-current side. Squid strips on the bottom hook and a Gulp on top has been the better combo when the current's really moving — squid holds up, plastic draws the strike. Axel Carlson Reef has been running the same pattern in slightly shallower water, 60 to 75 feet, and Shrewsbury Rocks up north is holding fish in that same range for boats working the northern end of the beat. None of this is a jumbo bite — these are solid, eating-size sea bass, plenty of shorts mixed in that need to go back — but it's a bite you can set a watch by, and that matters this time of year when a lot of other things offshore are inconsistent.

Triple Wrecks, the deeper stop in the network at 120 to 130 feet, has been holding the better average size. That extra depth and cooler water on the bottom seems to be keeping the bigger sea bass down there longer into the season, and reports have included fish pushing 4 pounds mixed in with the smaller stuff. If you want quality over quantity, that's the spot to burn the extra fuel for. Bonito have also been working the reef lines this week, chasing bait on top over Sea Girt and Shrewsbury — small metal jigs and epoxy jigs worked fast on light tackle have been the play for anyone who wants a change of pace from bottom fishing. That bonito run typically holds through the back half of September, so there's a window left on that one.

Now the harder truth: the tuna bite off Barnegat Ridge and out toward the Klondike has been thin and scattered this week, and it's worth being straight about that instead of dressing it up. The deep structure out there is still holding bait and there are fish around, but the reports coming back have been spotty — a fish here, a blown-up spread there, nothing that qualifies as a pattern you can plan a trip around yet. Bluefin have been the tougher of the two to find; when boats have connected, it's been on jigged diamond jigs and Ronz-style soft plastics worked over structure rather than trolled spreads, which tells you the fish are holding tight to bottom relief rather than roaming and feeding on top. That's a jig-and-drop game, not a run-and-gun troll game, at least for now.

The why here is pretty simple. The warm water pattern that's been carrying the better offshore tuna and mahi fishing further out has stayed remarkably stable for going on three weeks now, and that stability is exactly what's kept whatever tuna are working the Ridge and the Klondike in a holding pattern rather than pushing hard into our zone in numbers. We flagged this pattern last week — that the whole bite out there hinges on that warm water staying put — and that's exactly what's playing out. As long as it holds, there's no reason to expect a sudden surge of fish onto our structure; the moment it breaks down, that's when things could either improve fast or go quiet altogether. Worth watching, not worth planning a whole week around.

Looking at the next few days, the swell state offshore should stay manageable if the pattern holds, which keeps the reef bite the smart play. Best window is going to be the last two hours of the incoming tide through the top of the high — that's when the current on Sea Girt and Axel Carlson slows enough to fish bait effectively without getting blown off the wreck. Blackfish season in ocean waters hasn't opened yet, so that pressure hasn't hit the reef pieces, which is part of why the sea bass numbers have stayed healthy — no competition for the structure yet. Once tog season opens in a few weeks, expect that sea bass bite to get split with anglers working jigs and green crab for tautog on the same pieces.

If there's only one day to fish this week, make it Sea Girt Reef or Axel Carlson Reef on the last of the incoming tide, squid-and-Gulp combo, and don't bother running out past Barnegat Ridge unless there's a specific report in hand — the deep water tuna game right now is a bonus fish, not a target you can bank a trip on.
